post.title: Commit Wave Visualizer
post.hook: A repo's git history, drawn as one breathing green and red wave.
post.summary: XO Visualizer renders a git branch as a flowing Canvas 2D wave, additions rising green and deletions falling red. It grew from a histography-inspired viewer into a tool that can also run the working tree and spawn experiment worktrees.
post.writeup:
## What it is
XO Visualizer is a calm, histography-style view of a repo's history. Pick a branch in the sidebar and the stage draws it as a single flowing wave: additions rise above the centre line as a green ridge, deletions fall below as red. Point it at any local repo by absolute path, or leave it on the built-in synthetic sample data.

## Why
The goal was the feeling of histography.io: dark, smooth, organic, always gently moving. The repo includes a teardown of that site and a playbook for matching its finesse on a commit chart.

## How it works
Each commit adds a soft Gaussian bump, and the bumps are summed across the width into a ridge. Heights use `value^0.6` compression so huge commits do not flatten everything else. A slow traveling ripple makes the wave breathe, and on branch switch or Replay it streams in left to right with an ease-out reveal. Hovering snaps to the nearest commit and shows subject, additions, deletions, hash, author and date.

All git access is server-side. Route Handlers shell out through `execFile` (no shell, so paths cannot inject commands) and return normalized commit lists. The browser never touches the filesystem. Rendering is plain Canvas 2D with no charting dependencies, on Next.js 16, React 19 and Tailwind v4.

## Where it went
Version 0.2.0 (2026-06-08) added a split-pane run panel that shows the working tree live beside the wave, a dev-server process manager, a working-state readout, and an Experiment button. That button creates a git worktree on a new `experiment/N` branch and opens a Claude Code session in it.

## Open questions
History loads lazily in Fibonacci-sized batches, and it is not yet clear how the wave scales on very large repos. The repo has 2 commits so far, so it is early.
